description: Somos uma equipe jovens constituída por Devs, analista de dados e maketeiros
summary: RedMap is a website that brings together satellite data from NASA (NISAR, MODIS, VIIRS, SMAP, GPM) and agencies such as the USGS to show wildfires, floods, earthquakes, and storms on a simple map, both worldwide and in your region. A Trained Agent via Machine Learning, using data collected since 2000, estimates the risk for today, tomorrow, and the days ahead, and the site explains in plain language what to do.
details:
RedMap: Turning NASA Earth Observation into Local Risk Awareness

Live: https://redmap.handnexus.com (English at /en/)

Event: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Challenge of origin: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots

1. Summary

RedMap is a free, bilingual web app that works on any phone. It gathers NASA Earth observation data into a single map that tells people what is happening where they live, what may happen next, and what to do about it. It shows:

live wildfires, earthquakes, storms, volcanoes and floods;

a short-term forecast for today, tomorrow and in 2 days;

a machine learning forecast trained on NASA and USGS data;

NISAR radar change detection;

alerts and a preparedness guide.

The whole app runs in the browser. It has no login, collects no personal data and costs nothing per user.

2. The problem

Scattered, technical data. NASA publishes a lot of hazard data: FIRMS, GIBS, EONET, POWER, CMR and NISAR through ASF. Each one has its own portal, format and vocabulary, mostly in English. A resident, a teacher or a municipal civil defense officer rarely uses them.

Two fire satellites that cannot be compared directly. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) count hot spots differently because their pixel size and sensitivity differ. Combining them naively creates false trends in the fire record.

No local forecast that is easy to read and states its accuracy. Most risk tools are either expert-only or give a single color with no stated uncertainty.

Uneven exposure. In Brazil and much of Latin America, fire seasons, floods and landslides hit communities that have little access to technical warnings.

3. The solution

RedMap has four tabs: Observe, Forecast, Guide and Settings.

3.1 Observe (live)

Hot spots: last 24 hours from NASA FIRMS (MODIS Terra/Aqua, VIIRS Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21). The panel shows the time of the file in use.

Earthquakes: live M4.5+ from the USGS ComCat GeoJSON feed.

Natural events: last 30 days from NASA EONET v3 (wildfires, severe storms, volcanoes, floods, landslides, drought, dust and haze, extreme temperatures, sea and lake ice).

Severity: each event gets a level from 1 to 4, and a world ranking lists the most serious ones.

Satellite layers from NASA GIBS:

MODIS true color, 3-day flood, NDVI, land surface temperature and aerosols

VIIRS true color and Black Marble night lights

GPM IMERG rain rate

SMAP root-zone soil moisture (level 4)

OPERA DIST-ALERT (vegetation disturbance), DSWx-S1 (radar surface water) and RTC-S1

GPW v4 population density

Base map: OpenStreetMap, CARTO and Esri imagery, AWS Terrain 3D relief, and a globe or flat view.

Place panel: rain, soil wetness, temperature and humidity from NASA POWER. It also counts the recent NISAR, OPERA and VIIRS products over the place (NASA CMR, last 30 days).

3.2 Forecast

Today (next 5 hours), Tomorrow, In 2 days. Uses the hourly Open-Meteo forecast (ICON ensemble, DWD/ECMWF/ERA5 based), refreshed every 5 minutes. Fixed, published rules:

rain of 8, 15, 30 and 50 mm per day sets levels 1 to 4;

for fire, heat of 30 °C or more, humidity of 30% or less and wind of 20 km/h or more each add risk, and all three together give level 3.

AI forecast: chance of intense fire, flood, M4.5+ and M6+ earthquakes, and aftershocks (Section 5). For the short windows, the flood model is recomputed with forecast rain, and earthquake chances are converted from 30-day to 7-day rates with a Poisson model.

"How the AI was trained": a panel that shows each model's accuracy on data it never saw.

3.3 NISAR radar

What it is: NISAR (NASA–ISRO, L- and S-band SAR, launched 2025) sees the ground day and night and through clouds.

Finding scenes: RedMap searches the ASF DAAC for NISAR GCOV passes over the place.

Change detection: it compares two dates on the same track, directly in the browser. HH and HV backscatter are compared cell by cell, and neighboring changed cells are grouped into candidate changes.

Other products: it also counts interferogram (GUNW) and soil moisture (SME2) products.

Limits: the result is a triage on an uncalibrated 8-bit preview, and the app says it needs expert confirmation.

3.4 Alerts and preparedness

Alerts: in-browser notifications for the chosen place and an alert history. A red alert with recommendations appears only above a high confidence threshold.

Preparedness guide: an emergency kit checklist and guidance on what to do before, during and after each hazard.

Optional mailer: sends Telegram or e-mail alerts through GitHub Actions. It is turned off in the public version.

3.5 Settings

Theme and language.

An "Official sources and data" section that lists every satellite, database and service used. Each entry has its agency, what it measures, how RedMap uses it, how often it updates, and links to the source and its documentation.

4. Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS (the original challenge)

Overlap period: February 2012 onward, when both sensors operate.

Fit: an ordinary least squares fit in log space, between monthly MODIS counts and monthly VIIRS counts.

Train and test: fitted on 2012–2019, tested on 2020 onward, never on the same data.

Result: MODIS counts from 2000 onward are converted into "VIIRS-equivalent" counts, which gives one consistent fire record from 2000 to 2026.

Data published:

a harmonized timeline per 0.5° cell and month (one file per year, 2000–2026);

a fire calendar for the pilot region (Central Brazil), with the ratio of each month to its usual value;

a CSV for download.

First product: Firemap, "the fire calendar for any city". It is still available at /?landing.

5. Machine learning models we built

5.1 Method

Algorithm: gradient-boosted decision trees with XGBoost 3.4.1, binary logistic objective.

Settings: shallow trees (max depth 3), learning rate 0.08, subsampling 0.8, minimum child weight 10, L2 regularization 2.0.

Training: in Google Colab (notebooks/redmap_ia.py), with public NASA and USGS data downloaded at training time. Last training: 15 November 2026.

Honest validation: every train/test split is by time (train on older years, test on recent years) or by place (test on places never seen). No random split.

Runs in the browser: the trained trees are exported to JSON (web/data/ai/redmap_ai.json) and evaluated by ai.js with live data. The JavaScript output matches Python to 1e-16. No server and no data leaves the device.

Fallback: if the model files are unavailable, predict.js uses probability models with a declared basis.

5.2 Models

Fire (368 trees)

Predicts: chance of an intense fire month (10+ VIIRS-equivalent hot spots) in a 0.5° cell.

Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS + VIIRS, harmonized) and NASA POWER monthly climate.

Inputs:

hot spots in the previous 1–3 months, the same month last year, and the usual count for that month;

rain in the previous 1 and 3 months, and the rain anomaly;

soil wetness and its change;

temperature and humidity.

No-history case: in 40% of training rows the fire history is erased, so the model also works from climate alone in places with no fire record.

Training area: 786 cells in Central Brazil (lon −60 to −43.5, lat −20 to −7.5), November 2000 to October 2026.

Most important inputs: rain in the last month (32%), rain in the last 3 months (23%), the usual count for that month (15%) and last month's fires (13%).

Flood (109 trees)

Predicts: a flood risk index for the next 7 days.

How it learns: for every flood recorded by NASA EONET, it downloads the daily NASA POWER series at that place. It then compares the days before the flood with ordinary days at the same place.

Inputs:

rain over 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days, the 7-day maximum, and the ratio of 30-day rain to normal;

root-zone and topsoil wetness, and the 7-day change in root-zone wetness;

temperature and humidity;

forecast rain for the next 3 days.

Most important input: forecast rain for the next 3 days (46%).

Earthquake M4.5+ (308 trees) and M6+ (70 trees)

Predicts: chance of a quake in a 5° × 5° box in the next 30 days.

Data: the USGS catalog since 2000.

Inputs: quake counts in the last 30 days, the last year and the last 10 years, plus M6+ counts in the last year and the last 10 years.

Aftershock M5+ (127 trees) and M6+ (38 trees)

Predicts: chance of at least one aftershock within 7 days after an M6+, inside the rupture radius, max(50 km, 2 × 10^(0.5M − 1.85)).

Inputs: magnitude, depth, time elapsed, aftershocks so far, foreshocks in the previous 30 days and background activity over the last year.

Scientific basis: Reasenberg & Jones (1989), Science 243.

5.3 Validation on data the models never saw

Model Test set AUC Accuracy "Never happens" baseline

Fire (month) 2023–2026 0.886 81% 63%

Earthquake M4.5+ (30 days) 2021–2026 0.927 91% 86%

Earthquake M6+ (30 days) 2021–2026 0.925 99% 99%

Aftershock M5+ (7 days) 2019–2026 0.882 84% 74%

Aftershock M6+ (7 days) 2019–2026 0.861 95% 94%

Flood (7 days) 20% of places never seen 0.686 87% 87%

How to read the table: AUC is the chance that the model scores a real event above a non-event (0.5 means chance level). Overall accuracy is misleading for rare events, so we always show the "it never happens" baseline next to it.

Earthquake calibration: when the M4.5+ model says 35%, the event happened 34% of the time; when it says 85%, it happened 85% of the time.

Fire calibration: the model slightly overstates the top of the scale; it says 85% and the event happened 73% of the time.

Flood (stated weakness): at level 4 it catches 8% of floods with a 1.2% false alarm rate; at level 2, 30% with 11%.

Limit: training used observed rain, but the live site uses forecast rain, so real-world performance may be somewhat lower.

6. Data sources (complete list)

6.1 NASA satellites and instruments

NISAR (NASA JPL / ISRO): L- and S-band SAR; GCOV, GUNW and SME2 products. https://nisar.jpl.nasa.gov/

MODIS (Terra, Aqua): daily since 2000; imagery, flood, NDVI, land surface temperature, aerosols, hot spots. https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/instruments/modis

VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21): 375 m active fire, imagery, night lights. https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/instruments/viirs

GPM IMERG (NASA / JAXA): rain every 30 minutes. https://gpm.nasa.gov/data/imerg

SMAP (NASA JPL): root-zone soil moisture, level 4. https://smap.jpl.nasa.gov/

OPERA (NASA JPL; Sentinel-1, Landsat and Sentinel-2 HLS): DIST-ALERT, DSWx-S1, RTC-S1. https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/projects/opera

6.2 NASA databases and services

NASA FIRMS (LANCE): near-real-time hot spots and archive. https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/

NASA GIBS: satellite imagery as map tiles. https://nasa-gibs.github.io/gibs-api-docs/

NASA EONET v3: curated natural events. https://eonet.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/v3

NASA POWER (Langley; satellites + MERRA-2): daily and monthly climate. https://power.larc.nasa.gov/docs/

NASA CMR (Earthdata Search): product catalog. https://cmr.earthdata.nasa.gov/search/site/docs/search/api.html

ASF DAAC: NISAR scene search and previews. https://docs.asf.alaska.edu/api/basics/

GPW v4 (SEDAC / CIESIN): population density, 2020. https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/projects/gpw

Black Marble (NASA Goddard): night lights, cities and outages. https://blackmarble.gsfc.nasa.gov/

6.3 Other official and scientific sources

USGS earthquakes (ComCat): https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/

Open-Meteo (DWD ICON, ECMWF, Copernicus ERA5): forecast and climate history. https://open-meteo.com/en/docs

Reasenberg & Jones (1989): aftershock model. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.243.4895.1173

6.4 Maps and place names

OpenStreetMap (ODbL): https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright

CARTO basemaps: https://carto.com/basemaps

Esri World Imagery: https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=10df2279f9684e4a9f6a7f08febac2a4

AWS Terrain Tiles: https://registry.opendata.aws/terrain-tiles/

Open-Meteo Geocoding (GeoNames): https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/geocoding-api

BigDataCloud reverse geocoding: https://www.bigdatacloud.com/free-api/free-reverse-geocode-to-city-api. Only public event coordinates are sent, never the user's position.

7. Architecture and data storage

Front end

Static HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript; no framework and no build step.

MapLibre GL JS 5.6 for the map.

A strict Content-Security-Policy that forbids inline scripts.

Security headers: HSTS, nosniff, frame blocking and a restrictive Permissions-Policy.

Data pipeline

Python scripts refresh the FIRMS hot spots every hour (scheduled task) and build the harmonized timeline and calendar.

They publish to static hosting (HostGator) over FTPS.

The AI is retrained in Google Colab and published from there.

Database and storage

There is no traditional database and no user accounts. Everything served is static JSON:

hot spots from the last 24 hours;

the 2000–2026 harmonized timeline;

the AI models and the monthly fire grid;

OpenStreetMap infrastructure.

On the device: only preferences (theme, language, place, layers, alerts, kit checklist) and short-lived caches, stored in localStorage and sessionStorage.

Location: no IP geolocation; the user's location is used only if they allow GPS.

8. Audience

People living in areas exposed to fire, floods, earthquakes and storms.

Municipal governments and civil defense.

Schools and teachers.

Journalists and researchers.

The interface is in Portuguese and English. It switches to English automatically for devices set to another language or in U.S. time zones.

9. Origin and inspiration

Challenge of origin: RedMap started from the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots". Our first product was Firemap, a harmonized fire calendar per city.

Expansion: we then extended it into a multi-hazard map and added the new NISAR radar mission.

Inspiration: the project was inspired by work that team member Cícero did at Rumo Logística, the largest grain carrier in Latin America. His project was validated inside the company and won Brazil's national CCQ (Quality Control Circles) award and the UBQ 2026 award. From it we took a principle: a solution must be tested in real conditions before people are asked to trust it. That is why every RedMap forecast reports its accuracy on data it never saw.

10. NASA questions

What does it do or how does it work?

RedMap places NASA Earth observation data on one map and turns it into local risk awareness:

live hazards (FIRMS, USGS, EONET);

satellite layers (GIBS);

local climate (POWER);

a short-term forecast;

AI forecasts for fire, flood, earthquakes and aftershocks;

NISAR radar change detection;

alerts and a preparedness guide.

XGBoost models trained in Google Colab on NASA and USGS data are exported to JSON and evaluated in the browser with live data. The app needs no server and keeps no personal data.

What benefits does it have?

It is free and works on any phone.

It is bilingual and needs no login.

It turns technical data into plain language and severity levels from 1 to 4.

It provides a consistent MODIS and VIIRS fire history from 2000 to 2026.

It states its accuracy honestly: AUC 0.86–0.93 for fire and earthquakes on unseen years.

It lists every source with links.

What is the intended impact?

We want people and local governments to act before disasters, not only after them: know today's risk, receive an alert, and have a kit and a plan. We also want open NASA science to reach communities that never visit a scientific portal, starting in Brazil and Latin America.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python.

Libraries: MapLibre GL JS, XGBoost, pandas and NumPy.

NASA data and services: FIRMS, GIBS, EONET, POWER, CMR, ASF DAAC (NISAR), GPM IMERG, SMAP, OPERA, Black Marble and GPW.

Other data: USGS, Open-Meteo and OpenStreetMap.

Development and operations: Google Colab for training, GitHub, VS Code, Node.js, Microsoft Word for documentation, and HostGator static hosting deployed over FTPS.

Hardware: a Windows 11 PC.

AI coding assistant: Claude Code by Anthropic, with the Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 models. It was used to speed up development, as the Space Apps rules allow; the idea and all decisions are the team's.

AI for the project video and audio: Claude Opus 5.5 (high effort setting) was also used to create the project video and its audio. As with the code, the idea, the content and all decisions are the team’s.

How is your project creative?

Machine learning runs entirely in the browser: no server, no cost per user, and no data leaves the device.

Five hazards share one map, and each has its own published validation.

Two generations of fire satellites are combined into one 26-year record.

A brand-new radar mission, NISAR, is made usable by non-experts.

The site shows hit rates and limits instead of promising certainty.

The language is chosen automatically, with no tracking.

What factors did your team consider?

Privacy: no accounts, no IP location, no personal data.

Cost: free data and static hosting.

Access: works on weak mobile connections, with accessibility and two languages.

Security: CSP and security headers.

Scientific honesty: time- and place-based validation, calibration, and stated weaknesses (flood, uncalibrated NISAR preview).

False alarms: fixed, published thresholds, and red alerts only at high confidence.

Responsibility: RedMap does not issue official warnings and says so in the app.

Space Apps rules: Space Apps rules: original team idea, AI used only as an accelerator, including for the code, the video and the audio, and disclosed here.

11. Known limits

Hot spots are detections, not burned area.

NISAR change detection needs two passes and expert confirmation.

Probabilities are estimates, not official warnings.

The flood model is the weakest and was trained with observed rain, not forecast rain.

Alerts and history are stored per browser.
